sources.entry: attrs - Replacement for init, eq, repr, etc. boilerplate in class definitions.

summary.one_liner: attrs is a Python package with a class decorator that generates boilerplate dunder methods (such as __init__, __repr__, and equality checks) from declared attributes.
summary.what_it_does: The README describes attrs as a class decorator plus a declarative way to define class attributes. From those declarations it generates an initializer, a human-readable __repr__, equality-checking methods, and more. The example shows @define with type-annotated fields and Factory defaults, plus asdict() for converting an instance to a dict and make_class() for creating a class dynamically. Types are optional: fields can be declared with attrs.field() instead of annotations. The README says it differs from dataclasses in offering NumPy-aware equality checks, more hooks into initialization, a replacement for __init_subclass__, and debugger-friendly generated methods. It also notes that the classic APIs (@attr.s, attr.ib) and the attr import name will remain indefinitely.
use_cases: Writing concise data-holder classes without hand-coding __init__ and __repr__
Generating equality comparison for value-style classes
Converting class instances to dictionaries with asdict
Creating classes dynamically from a list of attribute names
Defining class attributes without type annotations using field()
Replacing dataclasses in projects needing more flexibility
notable: Modern @define API with optional type annotations, plus classic @attr.s and attr.ib APIs kept indefinitely
Declarative attribute definitions with generated repr, equality, and initializer
NumPy-aware equality checks and a replacement for __init_subclass__, per the README
Generated methods can be stepped through in a debugger
Trusted by NASA for Mars missions since 2020, per the README
caveats: The README does not state a license; the license field is set to unknown
Some advanced features are only described in external documentation and comparison pages, not in the README itself
